options: An electron in the outermost shell of an atom
An electron in the inner shells only
questions.explanation: A valence electron is specifically an electron in the outermost shell — the outer layer of the atom.
questions.misconception: Electrons in the inner shells are NOT valence electrons, and protons are not electrons at all — valence electrons are only the ones in the outermost shell.

questions.prompt: What role do valence electrons play in chemical bonding?
options: They are the electrons shared or transferred when atoms bond
They add weight to the atom
They have no role at all
questions.explanation: Valence electrons are the ones involved in bonding — shared in covalent bonds, transferred in ionic bonds.
questions.misconception: The nucleus is held by nuclear forces, not electrons, and inner electrons add bulk but do not bond — the bonding action belongs to the valence electrons.

questions.prompt: What does the number of valence electrons decide?
options: How many bonds an atom can form and how reactive it is
questions.explanation: The count of valence electrons sets how many bonds an atom can form and drives its reactivity.
questions.misconception: Mass comes from the nucleus, and color and temperature are unrelated — the valence electron count is what controls bonding behavior.

questions.prompt: Why do elements in the same column of the periodic table behave alike?
options: They have the same number of valence electrons
They are all the same temperature
They were discovered in the same year
questions.explanation: Elements in the same column (group) share the same number of valence electrons, and valence electrons drive bonding behavior.
questions.misconception: Elements in a column have different masses, but their bonding behavior matches because their OUTER electron count is identical.
